data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The cross-city variation in the nocturnal UHI is controlled by city size and the resulting urban heat island 'island effect': larger cities create a stronger internal boundary layer that inhibits radiative cooling, so the night-time gap scales with urban population and built extent.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If wind speeds are high enough to break down the urban boundary layer, city size would not modulate the UHI.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If small, dense cities show stronger UHI than large, sprawling ones, the city-size mechanism is invalid.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the UHI magnitude correlates more with street canyon geometry than total urban area, the boundary-layer scaling is secondary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A large city generates a distinct urban boundary layer (UBL) that decouples surface air from the regional atmosphere. The physical extent of the city determines the depth and persistence of this UBL. A larger city creates a thicker, more stable warm air dome that suppresses turbulent mixing and radiative cooling at the surface. The night-time gap therefore scales with city size: larger built extents produce a more pronounced UHI because the internal boundary layer is stronger and more effective at retaining heat.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
